explanations.explanation: Paul says, "I bow my knees before the Father" (Ephesians 3:14). That's how he comes to Him. I don't have knees, so I'd have to bow the whole hat, and my mustache would have to catch it before it hit the counter.

Paul doesn't mention lifting hands here. He says, "I bow my knees before the Father" (Ephesians 3:14). My hands are my mustache, so lifting them means lifting a mustache, and that gets tired fast, friend.

There's no singing in this verse. Paul says, "I bow my knees before the Father" (Ephesians 3:14), so he's bowing, not standing. That's probably for the best, because my singing sounds like a mixer with a loose bolt.

Paul asks that out of the riches of His glory the Father "may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). Strength is the first thing in his prayer. Notice it's the kind of strength you can't see from the outside, and that's the kind I'd want on the days my edges feel soft.

That's not what Paul asks for here. He asks that the Father "may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). He asks for strength inside them, and that's the request he puts first.

An easy life sounds lovely, like dough that rolls itself out. But Paul doesn't ask for it in this prayer. He asks that the Father "may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16).

Paul says the Father "may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). The power comes through the Spirit, and it lands deep inside. My inner being is mostly dough, so I'd take all the help I can get.

Paul is an apostle himself (Ephesians 1:1), and he doesn't say "through me." He says the power comes "through His Spirit" (Ephesians 3:16). Friend, he had the perfect spot to hand himself some credit, and he walked right past it.

Prophets show up in Ephesians 3:5, where the mystery is revealed to His holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit. So the Spirit is in that verse too. But in this prayer, the strengthening comes "through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). Prophets are great, they're just not the answer on this one.

explanations.answer: Christ may dwell in their hearts
explanations.explanation: Paul asks for that strength "so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Ephesians 3:17). "Dwell" is a living-there word, not a stopping-by word. So the strength in the inner being leads right to Christ making His home in their hearts.

Paul never brings up enemies in this prayer. He says, "so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Ephesians 3:17). The goal is about who lives in the heart, not who's left standing at the end.

explanations.answer: They may earn a great reward
explanations.explanation: There's no prize table in this prayer, friend. Paul says, "so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Ephesians 3:17). Christ dwelling in their hearts is the very thing he names.

Not quite, friend. Paul says they will have power "together with all the saints" to comprehend it (Ephesians 3:18). Nobody's grasping this one alone. I tried to stamp a whole tray by myself once, and my mustache needed a nap.

False is right. Paul says they'll have power, "together with all the saints," to comprehend it (Ephesians 3:18). The picture is a whole crowd grasping it, not one person alone in a corner. Big jobs go better with company, and I've got the tangled mustache stories to prove it.

Love is right. Paul prays they'll comprehend "the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ" (Ephesians 3:18-19). That's four directions, all aimed at one thing. I'd need a way longer mustache just to measure it.

Kingdom is a big word, but it's not the one Paul uses here. He says they'll comprehend the length and width and height and depth "of the love of Christ" (Ephesians 3:18-19). His measuring tape is aimed at love.

Wisdom is a fine ingredient, but it's not in this recipe. Paul says they'll comprehend the length and width and height and depth "of the love of Christ" (Ephesians 3:18-19). The word he picks is love.

explanations.answer: It's bigger than our minds can hold
explanations.explanation: Paul calls it "this love that surpasses knowledge" (Ephesians 3:19). It goes past what we can know. Trying to take in all of it is like trying to hug a mountain with my mustache. And Paul still prays that they would know it, so it's worth reaching for.

explanations.answer: It's only for the very wise
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that. He prays they'll have power "together with all the saints" to comprehend the love of Christ (Ephesians 3:18). The love "surpasses knowledge" (Ephesians 3:19), so no one's smarts get them to the end of it. No smarts are required at the door.

explanations.answer: It fades once you learn it
explanations.explanation: Paul says nothing about it fading. He calls it "this love that surpasses knowledge," and he prays they'd be "filled with all the fullness of God" (Ephesians 3:19). Even after a whole lot of batches, my dough still gets me excited. A love that surpasses knowledge is a love you don't run out of knowing.

Paul says God is "able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine" (Ephesians 3:20). I've imagined some mighty big cookie boxes, and Paul says God goes past even that. He adds that it's "according to His power that is at work within us."
A little more would be a few extra sprinkles. Paul says "immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine" (Ephesians 3:20). That's way past a sprinkle, friend.

Exactly that much would call for a measuring cup, and Paul uses a word with no measuring in it. He says God is able to do "immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine" (Ephesians 3:20). Our asking and imagining don't set the limit.

explanations.answer: In the church and in Christ Jesus
explanations.explanation: Paul says, "to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 3:21). Those are the two places he names. He gives the address, and it's the church and Christ Jesus.
Paul doesn't name the temple here. He says, "to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 3:21). That's the address he gives, with no street name needed.

Paul doesn't put the glory there in this verse. He says, "to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 3:21). Heaven does come up earlier, when he says every family in heaven and on earth derives its name from the Father (Ephesians 3:15). But the glory in verse 21 is in the church and in Christ Jesus.

Not quite, friend. Paul says the glory goes to Him "throughout all generations, forever and ever" (Ephesians 3:21). That means way more than one generation. Glory for just one generation would be one tiny batch.

False is right. Paul says, "to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever" (Ephesians 3:21). It's not just for his own generation. Every generation gets in on it, and that's a whole lot of batches.
